title: Every seat tints whoever sits there
allegory: Attention is a table where every word can look at every other word at once, but nobody has a seat number; a positional embedding hangs a learned coloured lamp over each seat, and whoever sits there takes on its tint, so the others can tell where each word sat.
map: words round a table, all looking at each other at once
tokens in attention: every query is compared with every key
with no lamps, swapping two guests changes nothing anyone sees
attention alone is order-blind: shuffle the tokens and the outputs just shuffle
a coloured lamp over seat i, its colour picked by practice
W_pos[i]: a learned vector for position i
the word's own colour blended with its seat's tint
x₀ = W_E[token] + W_pos[i], added into the residual stream
a late guest told they are in seat 0
the KV-cache bug: W_pos[0] added to a token that really sits at position 47

cap.1: Dog bites man, man bites dog: same words, very different news. Attention on its own compares words by what they are, not where they sit.
cap.2: Attention scores depend only on query and key contents. Shuffle the input tokens and, with no position information, the outputs just shuffle with them.
cap.3: Unmasked attention is permutation-equivariant: permuting inputs permutes outputs. A causal mask leaks a little order on its own, but GPT-2 supplies position explicitly with W_pos.

cap.1: Hang a coloured lamp over every seat. Whoever sits in seat 2 is tinted by seat 2's lamp, so everyone can see where each word sat.
cap.2: PosEmbed is a lookup table W_pos with one learned vector per position. Each token gets its position's vector added to its word vector.
cap.3: W_pos has shape (n_ctx, d_model). PosEmbed takes W_pos[:seq_len] and repeats it over the batch: the same position always gets the same vector, whatever the token.

cap.1: The tint is mixed in, not pinned on. Each word enters the model as its own colour plus its seat's colour: one blended vector.
cap.2: The residual stream starts as token embedding plus positional embedding. Same width, simply added, so every later layer reads one vector per position.
cap.3: x₀ = W_E[t] + W_pos[i] puts content and position in one d_model space. Heads can then read position through W_Q and W_K, as the previous-token head 0.7 does.

chapters.name: A head reads seats
chapters.title: a previous-token head, idealised (rows look at columns)

cap.1: Because seats have colours, a word can learn 'always look at the seat just before mine'. Here each row finds the word one seat back.
cap.2: In [1.2] you compute a previous-token head's attention from positional embeddings alone, and it shows this clean band just below the diagonal.
cap.3: The positional QK circuit W_pos W_QK W_posᵀ for head 0.7, after masking, scaling and softmax, concentrates on the sub-diagonal: position i attends to i-1.

chapters.name: The late guest
chapters.verdict: With a cache, index W_pos from the cached length, not from zero.

cap.1: A speed trick: remember the earlier guests and seat only the newcomer. Forget to tell them their real seat and they get seat 0's tint every time.
cap.2: With a KV cache you pass one token, so its index is 0 and PosEmbed adds W_pos[0]. Nothing errors; the text just drifts. Use W_pos[cached_len:].
cap.3: Cached and uncached generation agree on the first token, then diverge. Index W_pos[cached_len : cached_len + n_new], then assert identical token ids with and without the cache.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Previous-token heads read the seat colours
Induction heads are built on top of them

cap.1: Order lets a model spot patterns like 'what came after this word last time'. Those skills start with a head that reads the seat colours.
cap.2: Previous-token heads use positional embeddings to look one step back, and induction heads build on them. The [4.3] reasoning model uses RoPE, which rotates queries and keys instead.
cap.3: Positional structure is the substrate of the first circuits you reverse-engineer: previous-token into induction via K-composition. Knowing where order enters tells you where to look to read or steer it.

coda.title: Who bit whom? A toy head at the last word looks back along the seats

params.label: Sentence: dog bites man (0) or man bites dog (1)

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: (v => abs(v) < 0.05 ? 'cannot tell' : (v > 0 ? 'the dog did it' : 'the man did it'))(dot(softmax([0, -alpha, -2*alpha]), order < 0.5 ? [1, 0, -1] : [-1, 0, 1]))

caption.1: Lamps off: the last word hears dog and man equally and cannot tell who bit whom. Turn the lamps up, then flip the sentence.
caption.2: At alpha 0 this toy head is order-blind: both sentences read 0. Raise alpha and it looks to seat 0, where the biter sits, so the two sentences finally differ.
caption.3: Toy head with score_j = -alpha·j from position alone. At alpha = 0 the output is invariant to word order; position-dependent scores only exist because W_pos was added.

where_else: Previous-token heads, which look one step back using positional embeddings alone
Induction heads, built on previous-token heads through K-composition
KV caching, where the position index must continue from the cached length
RoPE in newer models such as the [4.3] reasoning model: position by rotating queries and keys

hamming.what: A learned vector for each position, added to each token's embedding so the model knows where every word sits.
hamming.when: At the very start of every forward pass, and again with care whenever you generate with a KV cache.
hamming.why: Attention compares only contents, so without position the model could not tell dog bites man from man bites dog.

object.title: The lamp-lit table
object.subtitle: Three seats, three words: each row is a word's vector, tinted by the lamp over its seat.

knobs.label: dog bites man (0) or man bites dog (1)

cap.1: Three seats, three words, no lamps. Each row is just the word's own colour: dog, bites, man.
cap.2: Token embeddings only: row i is W_E[token at position i].
cap.3: x₀ without W_pos: each row depends on the token alone.

cap.1: Swap dog and man. The rows simply trade places; nothing in a row says where it sat.
cap.2: Without position, reordering tokens only permutes the rows. The set of vectors is unchanged.
cap.3: Permutation of inputs gives the same permutation of x₀: nothing downstream can recover order from content.

cap.1: Lamps on. Every row picks up its seat's tint, so each row now carries where it sat.
cap.2: x₀ = W_E[token] + W_pos[i]: the same seat adds the same tint whatever word sits there.
cap.3: W_pos[i] is added per position and broadcast over the batch; content and position share d_model.

cap.1: Swap again. Dog in seat 2 no longer looks like dog in seat 0: order has become visible.
cap.2: Now reordering changes the vectors themselves, so attention scores can depend on position.
cap.3: With W_pos, x₀ is no longer permutation-equivariant in the tokens, which is what lets QK read order.

cap.1: Dim the lamps and the tint shrinks. It is always blended into the same numbers as the word, never stacked beside it.
cap.2: Addition, not concatenation: the positional signal lives in the same dimensions as the word signal.
cap.3: Because x₀ is a sum, later components must separate position from content by reading different directions.

predict.q: With no positional embedding, you swap two words. What happens to attention's outputs?

options.t: They swap places too; nothing else changes

predict.why: Attention compares contents only, so shuffling the inputs only shuffles the outputs (the causal mask aside).

predict.q: With a KV cache, the token at position 47 arrives alone. Which positional vector should it get?

options.t: W_pos[0], since it is the first token in this call

predict.why: Its seat is its real place in the sequence. Index from the cached length, or the text quietly drifts.

predict.q: How is the seat's colour combined with the word's?

options.t: Attached as extra numbers on the end

predict.why: x₀ = W_E[token] + W_pos[i]: same width, simply summed, so content and position share one space.

object.where: Anywhere an order-blind mixer needs order: tokens in a transformer, and every KV-cached generation.
